items.text: Through interval manipulation and relative non-auditory cognitive tasks, the sensory versus memory/attention contributions in spectral ripple measurement are tested, rather than treating threshold differences directly as auditory resolution.

Comparisons of individual band weights, word/non-word, and binaural audibility can test whether average adult band importance applies to developing children with hearing loss, generating knowledge for individualized hearing assistance.

Two-year tracking and noise/two-talker competing speech comparisons study the immediate and cumulative relationships of audibility through language development; results such as non-significant mediation and stable weights can still refine theory.

Observational paths and growth models of cognition/language/audibility do not automatically identify causal mediation; age, reverse relationships, shared abilities, and measurement changes remain alternative explanations; interval manipulation only provides local causal constraints.

Band weights are relative contributions given a combination and audibility, not directly equivalent to active attention; sensory levels, hearing aid processing, and acoustic differences between competing speech and steady-state noise also mean the three tasks are not pure process measures.

Claims of very small d per experimental sample, complex mediation/multiple comparisons, heterogeneous hearing loss, and longitudinal attrition require explicit simulation assumptions to support; overall recruitment, per-study sample sizes, and some numbers in the table are also inconsistent.
